segments.text: Management is the process of getting organizational work done through four connected activities — planning, organizing, leading, and controlling — applied to people, money, materials, and information. Every other unit in this subject assumes this vocabulary: when Financial Management talks about “capital budgeting decisions,” it is really talking about a planning decision; when Marketing talks about “managing distribution channels,” it is really talking about an organizing decision. Getting comfortable with the language of this unit therefore pays off across the whole paper.

The unit itself moves through a logical sequence: it starts by defining what an organization and a manager actually are, then breaks down what managers do day to day (the four functions, Mintzberg’s roles, the skills mix), then looks outward at the environment managers must respond to, then looks at how managers plan and decide, then at how a whole organization sets long-term direction (strategy) and shapes itself structurally to carry that direction out, and finally at the human side of leading people through change, leadership, and motivation.

blocks.text: .2 Defining Organization, Management, and Management in Organizations

segments.text: An
organization

is a deliberately coordinated social unit, composed of two or more people, that functions on a relatively continuous basis to achieve a common goal or set of goals. Four elements are packed into that definition, and each one matters for later topics:

items.text: A distinct purpose.
Without a goal, there is nothing to coordinate toward — this is why every later planning and strategy topic starts from “what is the organization trying to achieve?”
People.
An organization is fundamentally social; one person working alone is not an organization in this sense, because there is no one to coordinate with.
A deliberate structure.

Work is divided among people (division of labour) and some formal system of roles, authority, and reporting relationships exists — this is the seed of the later topic on organizational structure and design.
Continuity.
An organization persists beyond any single transaction or project, which is why it needs ongoing management rather than a one-time decision.

segments.text: It is useful to separate the
formal organization
— the official structure of roles, rules, and authority shown on an organization chart — from the
informal organization

: the unofficial relationships, communication networks, and group norms that also shape how work actually gets done. A new manager who reads only the organization chart and ignores the informal network will misunderstand why some instructions are followed quickly and others are quietly resisted.
Management

is the process of coordinating and overseeing the work activities of others so that their activities are completed efficiently and effectively. Two words in that sentence carry almost all of the exam-relevant content:

items.text: Efficiency
means getting the most output from the least input — “doing things right.” A factory that produces the same output with less wasted material or labour has become more efficient.
Effectiveness

means completing activities so that organizational goals are attained — “doing the right things.” A factory that produces exactly the product the market wants, even if some resources are used loosely, is being effective.

segments.text: Management aims for both together. A manager who is highly efficient but ineffective (perfectly optimizing production of a product nobody wants) has failed just as clearly as one who is effective but wildly inefficient (delivering what the market wants at ruinous cost). Peter Drucker’s well-known distinction — “efficiency is doing things right; effectiveness is doing the right things” — is worth memorizing in exactly that phrasing, since examiners often test it directly.

blocks.text: .2.3 Management in organizations: who is a manager?

segments.text: A
manager
is someone who coordinates and oversees the work of other people so that organizational goals can be accomplished. Managers are commonly classified by level:

items.text: First-line (supervisory) managers
manage the work of non-managerial employees directly involved in producing the organization’s product or service — a shift supervisor on a factory floor, for example.
Middle managers
manage the work of first-line managers, translating top management’s broad strategy into departmental plans.
Top managers
are responsible for making organization-wide decisions and establishing plans and goals that affect the entire organization — a CEO or managing director.

segments.text: Key takeaways

items.text: An organization needs purpose, people, deliberate structure, and continuity; both its formal chart and its informal networks shape how work gets done.
Management is judged on both efficiency (doing things right, minimizing waste) and effectiveness (doing the right things, achieving goals) — high performance requires both together.
Managers are layered into first-line, middle, and top levels, each translating direction from above into more specific action below.

blocks.text: .3 The Four Management Functions, Managerial Roles, and Managerial Skills

segments.text: Henri Fayol’s classic framework, still the backbone of how management is taught, groups everything a manager does into four functions:

items.text: Planning

means defining goals, establishing an overall strategy for achieving them, and developing a comprehensive hierarchy of plans to integrate and coordinate activities. Planning answers “where are we going, and how do we get there?” before any resources are committed.
Organizing

means arranging and structuring work to accomplish an organization’s goals — deciding what tasks are to be done, who is to do them, how tasks are to be grouped, who reports to whom, and where decisions are to be made. Organizing turns a plan into an assignable structure of jobs and authority.
Leading

means working with and through people to accomplish goals — motivating subordinates, influencing individuals or teams as they work, selecting the most effective communication channels, and resolving conflicts. Leading is the function most concerned with the human, interpersonal side of getting work done, as distinct from the structural side (organizing).
Controlling

means monitoring activities to ensure they are being accomplished as planned and correcting any significant deviations. Controlling closes the loop back to planning: actual performance is compared against the goals set during planning, and gaps trigger either corrective action or a revision of the plan itself.

segments.text: These four functions are not a rigid one-time sequence performed once at the start of a project; they operate continuously and iteratively — a manager plans, then as work proceeds organizes and re-organizes, leads throughout, and controls constantly, feeding control information back into future planning.

Henry Mintzberg, based on direct observation of practising managers, argued that what managers actually spend their time on is better captured by ten roles grouped into three categories, rather than by the tidy four functions above:

items.text: Interpersonal roles
— figurehead (performing ceremonial and symbolic duties), leader (motivating and directing subordinates), and liaison (maintaining a network of contacts outside one’s own unit).
Informational roles

— monitor (seeking and receiving information to understand the organization and its environment), disseminator (transmitting information received from outsiders or subordinates to other members), and spokesperson (transmitting information to outsiders on the organization’s plans, policies, and results).
Decisional roles

— entrepreneur (initiating and overseeing new projects to improve performance), disturbance handler (taking corrective action when the organization faces unexpected difficulties), resource allocator (deciding where organizational resources are directed), and negotiator (representing the organization in major negotiations).

segments.text: The functions and the roles are not competing theories so much as two different lenses on the same job: the four functions describe the purpose of managerial activity, while Mintzberg’s roles describe the observed behaviour through which managers actually carry out that purpose.
Robert Katz identified three essential skill categories, and — importantly for the exam — the relative importance of each shifts as a manager rises through the organizational levels:

items.text: Technical skills
are the job-specific knowledge and proficiency needed to perform specialized tasks — most critical for first-line managers, who are closest to the actual technical work.
Human skills

are the ability to work well with other people, individually and in groups — important at every level, since all managers deal with people, but especially central at middle levels where coordination across units is constant.
Conceptual skills

are the ability to think and conceptualize about abstract and complex situations — to see the organization as a whole and understand how its parts relate to each other and to the wider environment. These become most critical at the top, where decisions involve the entire organization’s long-term direction.

segments.text: A useful way to remember the shift: technical skills matter most “close to the ground,” conceptual skills matter most “at altitude,” and human skills matter throughout because management is, at every level, fundamentally a social activity.
Key takeaways

items.text: The four functions — planning, organizing, leading, controlling — describe the continuous, iterative purpose of managerial work, with controlling feeding back into future planning.
Mintzberg’s ten roles (interpersonal, informational, decisional) describe the same job from the angle of observed day-to-day behaviour rather than abstract purpose.

Katz’s three skills — technical, human, conceptual — are all needed, but their relative weight shifts: technical matters most at the first-line level, conceptual matters most at the top, human skill matters throughout.

blocks.text: .4 The Organizational Internal and External Environment

segments.text: No organization exists in isolation. Everything a manager plans, organizes, leads, and controls happens inside a context that both constrains and creates opportunity — this context is the organizational
environment
, conventionally split into an internal and an external component.
The internal environment consists of factors inside the organization’s own boundary that managers have comparatively direct influence over:

items.text: Organizational culture

— the shared values, beliefs, and norms that influence how employees act, often described as “how things are done around here.” Culture is powerful precisely because it is often unwritten, yet it shapes decisions as strongly as formal policy.
Structure
— the formal arrangement of jobs and reporting relationships (developed further in the structure and design topic below).
Resources
— the financial, physical, human, and informational assets the organization has to work with.
Employees
— their skills, motivation, and the informal relationships among them.

segments.text: The external environment consists of forces outside the organization’s boundary that it typically cannot control directly, and must instead monitor and adapt to. It is useful to distinguish two layers:

items.text: The specific (task) environment

includes the parties an organization directly interacts with and that directly affect its ability to achieve goals — customers, suppliers, competitors, and pressure groups/regulators specific to its industry.
The general environment

includes broader conditions that may not have an immediate day-to-day effect but shape the context for everyone in the economy — economic conditions, technological trends, socio-cultural trends, demographic trends, political/legal conditions, and global conditions. A useful mnemonic for scanning the general environment is
PESTEL
: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, and Legal.

blocks.text: .4.4 Environmental uncertainty and how managers respond

segments.text: The practical exam-relevant point is not simply “list the environmental factors,” but explain
why

managers care: environmental uncertainty (a combination of environmental complexity — how many and how different are the elements — and environmental dynamism — how fast those elements change) determines how much active scanning, forecasting, and flexibility a manager must build into planning. A stable, simple environment (few competitors, slow-changing technology) allows fairly rigid long-term plans; a complex, dynamic environment (many competitors, rapid technological change) forces managers toward shorter planning horizons, more frequent environmental scanning, and organizational structures flexible enough to adapt quickly — a theme picked up again under “Designing Adaptive Organizations” below.
Key takeaways

items.text: The internal environment (culture, structure, resources, employees) is comparatively controllable; the external environment (task environment plus the broader PESTEL forces) is not, and must instead be monitored and adapted to.

Environmental uncertainty — a function of complexity and dynamism — is the key variable: more uncertainty pushes managers toward shorter planning horizons, continuous scanning, and more flexible structures.
The practical question managers ask is never just “what is changing?” but “how will this change affect our goals, costs, people, or customers, and what should we do differently as a result?”

blocks.text: .5 Management Planning, Goal Setting, and Decision Making

segments.text: Planning is the management function that involves defining an organization’s goals, establishing an overall strategy for achieving those goals, and developing plans to integrate and coordinate organizational work. Planning gives direction, reduces the impact of change by forcing managers to anticipate it, minimizes waste and redundancy, and sets the standards later used for controlling.
Plans differ along several dimensions worth distinguishing clearly:

items.text: Breadth
: strategic plans apply to the entire organization and set broad, long-term goals; operational plans specify the details of how overall goals are to be achieved.
Time frame
: long-term plans typically extend beyond three years; short-term plans cover one year or less.
Specificity
: specific plans are clearly defined and leave no room for interpretation; directional plans set out general guidelines and provide flexibility, at the cost of clarity.
Frequency of use

: single-use plans are designed for a one-time, non-repeating situation (a specific project); standing plans are ongoing and provide guidance for repeatedly performed activities (a policy or procedure).

segments.text: Goals are the desired outcomes toward which plans are directed. Well-designed goals are typically described using the
SMART

criteria — Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, and Time-bound — because a vague goal (“improve customer service”) cannot reliably guide action or be checked during controlling, while a SMART goal (“reduce average customer complaint resolution time to under 24 hours within the next two quarters”) can.
Two broad approaches to setting goals are contrasted in the syllabus:

items.text: Traditional goal setting

, in which goals are set at the top and then broken down into subgoals for each organizational level — a “cascade” that can lose meaning or urgency as it moves down through several layers if lower-level managers interpret the goal loosely.
Management by Objectives (MBO)

, a process in which specific performance goals are jointly determined by employees and their managers, progress toward the goals is periodically reviewed, and rewards are allocated based on that progress. MBO is designed to overcome the “lost in translation” problem of the traditional cascade by making goal-setting a joint, negotiated process at every level rather than a one-way instruction downward.

segments.text: A decision is a choice made from two or more alternatives, and decision making is the process of identifying problems and opportunities and then resolving them. The
rational decision-making model
describes an idealized, step-by-step process:

items.text: Identify the problem — the discrepancy between an existing and a desired state of affairs.
Identify the decision criteria — the factors relevant to resolving the problem.
Allocate weights to the criteria, reflecting their relative importance.
Develop a set of alternatives that could resolve the problem.
Analyze each alternative against the weighted criteria.
Select the alternative with the highest total score.
Implement the chosen alternative.
Evaluate the decision’s outcome, to see whether the problem was actually resolved.

segments.text: In practice, managers rarely follow this fully rational process, because of
bounded rationality

— the idea (associated with Herbert Simon) that decision-makers are limited by incomplete information, cognitive limitations, and time pressure, and so tend to construct simplified models that extract the essential features of problems without capturing their full complexity. Bounded rationality typically leads to
satisficing
— accepting the first alternative that is “good enough” against the criteria, rather than continuing to search for the theoretically optimal one.
Decisions are also usefully classified by the nature of the problem they respond to:

items.text: Programmed decisions
are repetitive and can be handled by a routine approach — an existing policy or procedure already tells the manager what to do (for example, how to process a standard leave application).
Non-programmed decisions
are unique, non-recurring, and require a custom-made solution, because no existing rule fully fits the novel situation (for example, how to respond to a sudden, unprecedented product-safety crisis).

segments.text: Managers are also affected by decision-making conditions that describe how much is known in advance:
certainty
(the outcome of each alternative is known in advance),
risk
(outcomes are not certain, but probabilities can be reasonably estimated), and
uncertainty
(the decision-maker has neither certainty about outcomes nor even reliable probability estimates to work with).
Key takeaways

items.text: Plans vary by breadth (strategic vs. operational), time frame, specificity (specific vs. directional), and frequency (single-use vs. standing) — matching the plan type to the situation is itself a managerial skill.
SMART goals can be tracked and controlled against; MBO tries to fix the “lost in translation” weakness of a top-down goal cascade by making goal-setting a joint process.

The rational decision-making model is an eight-step ideal; bounded rationality and satisficing describe how managers actually decide under real limits of information, cognition, and time. Decisions also vary by type (programmed vs. non-programmed) and by the certainty, risk, or uncertainty of the conditions surrounding them.

segments.text: Strategy is the set of managerial decisions and actions that determine the long-run performance of an organization. It is the mechanism by which an organization translates its overall purpose into a coherent, sustained pattern of choices about which markets to compete in and how to compete in them.

blocks.text: .6.2 The strategic management process, step by step

items.text: Identify the organization’s current mission, goals, and strategies.
The mission is a statement of an organization’s purpose — why it exists.
Conduct an external analysis.
Managers scan the general and specific (task) environments (the same environment discussed above) to identify opportunities (positive external trends) and threats (negative external trends).
Conduct an internal analysis.

Managers assess the organization’s resources, capabilities, and core competencies (activities the organization does particularly well) to identify strengths (things it does well relative to competitors) and weaknesses (things it does poorly or lacks).
Steps 2 and 3 together are commonly summarized as
SWOT analysis
— Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats — matching internal capability against external conditions.
Formulate strategies.
Strategies are developed at three levels:
corporate-level
strategy answers “what businesses should we be in?”;
business-level (competitive)
strategy answers “how should we compete in each of those businesses?”;
functional-level
strategy answers “how does each department (marketing, operations, finance) support the business-level strategy?” At the business level, Michael Porter’s generic strategies frame the central choice:
cost leadership
(being the lowest-cost producer in an industry),
differentiation
(offering unique products/services valued by customers, allowing a premium price), or
focus
(concentrating on a narrow market segment and pursuing either a cost or differentiation advantage within that segment specifically).
Implement strategies.

A strategy is only as good as the organization’s ability to execute it — this is where strategy connects directly to the later topics on organizational structure and change management, since structure and culture must be aligned with the chosen strategy.
Evaluate results.

How effective have the strategies been, and what adjustments are needed? This closes the loop, feeding back into a revised mission/goals/strategy statement, making strategic management an ongoing cycle rather than a one-time plan.

segments.text: Key takeaways

items.text: Strategic management is a continuous six-step cycle: assess current mission and strategy → external analysis (opportunities/threats) → internal analysis (strengths/weaknesses) → formulate strategy at corporate, business, and functional levels → implement → evaluate and feed back.
SWOT analysis is simply the combination of the external and internal analysis steps — do not treat it as a separate, unrelated technique.

Porter’s three generic business-level strategies (cost leadership, differentiation, focus) describe the fundamental choices about how to compete once which businesses to be in has been decided at the corporate level.

segments.text: Organizational structure is the formal arrangement of jobs within an organization. Organizational design is the process managers use to develop or change that structure. Six key elements are traditionally used to describe and design a structure:

items.text: Work specialization

— the degree to which tasks are subdivided into separate jobs (division of labour). High specialization can raise efficiency through repetition and focus, but excessive specialization can cause boredom, fatigue, and disengagement — a trade-off worth stating explicitly in an exam answer.
Departmentalization
— the basis by which jobs are grouped together, commonly by function (grouping by activity performed, e.g., marketing, finance), by product, by geography, by process, or by customer.
Chain of command
— the continuous line of authority that extends from upper organizational levels to the lowest levels, clarifying who reports to whom.
Span of control

— the number of employees a manager can efficiently and effectively direct; wider spans are efficient (fewer managers needed) but only work well when subordinates are well-trained and tasks are relatively similar and routine.
Centralization and decentralization

— centralization is the degree to which decision-making is concentrated at a single point (typically top management); decentralization pushes decision-making authority down toward lower levels, closer to where the relevant information and action actually occur.
Formalization
— the degree to which jobs are standardized and the extent to which employee behaviour is guided by rules and procedures.
Simple structure
— low departmentalization, wide spans of control, centralized authority; typical of small, young organizations.
Functional structure
— departmentalization by function; efficient for a single-product or narrow-line business but can create silos that make cross-functional coordination difficult.
Divisional structure

— made up of separate, semi-autonomous units or divisions, typically organized around products, geographies, or customer groups, each with fairly self-contained functional specialists; suits large, diversified organizations, at the cost of duplicating resources across divisions.

segments.text: Key takeaways

items.text: Structure is built from six elements — work specialization, departmentalization, chain of command, span of control, centralization/decentralization, and formalization — and every structural design question is really a question of how to combine these six.
The choice between functional and divisional structure trades efficiency and coordination (functional) against responsiveness and accountability per product/market (divisional).
Structure should follow strategy: a structure well-suited to a stable, single-product business will not automatically suit a diversified, fast-changing one.

segments.text: Building on the basic structural elements above, this topic addresses how structure changes when the environment is uncertain and fast-moving (recall the discussion of environmental uncertainty above).

items.text: Mechanistic organizations

are rigid and tightly controlled structures — high formalization, high centralization, narrow spans, extensive departmentalization — that work well in stable, predictable environments where efficiency through standardization is the priority.
Organic organizations

are highly adaptive and flexible structures — low formalization, decentralized decision-making, wide information-sharing — that work well in dynamic, uncertain environments where the organization must respond quickly to unexpected change.
Contingency thinking

ties this together: there is no single best structure; the right structure is contingent on the organization’s strategy, size, technology, and — as emphasized here — the degree of environmental uncertainty it faces. This is the structural expression of the same idea introduced when discussing environmental uncertainty above.

segments.text: Contemporary adaptive designs mentioned in the syllabus include the
team structure
, where the entire organization is made up of work teams that coordinate directly rather than through a rigid hierarchy, and the
boundaryless organization
, which seeks to eliminate internal (across departments) and external (with suppliers/customers) barriers to coordination — often enabled by information technology.
Key takeaways

items.text: Mechanistic structures suit stable environments (efficiency through standardization); organic structures suit dynamic environments (agility through decentralization).
Contingency theory holds that structural choice should follow the organization’s actual situation — its environment, strategy, size, and technology — rather than any single ideal blueprint.
Team-based and boundaryless designs are practical responses to high uncertainty, reducing the coordination cost of a rigid hierarchy.

blocks.text: .9.1 Forces for and resistance to change

segments.text: Organizations face constant pressure to change from both external forces (the environmental factors already discussed) and internal forces (a new strategy, a shift in the workforce, new equipment, changing employee attitudes). Employees commonly resist change for a set of well-documented reasons: uncertainty about the effects of the change, fear of losing something already valued (status, income, established routines), or a belief that the change is inconsistent with existing organizational goals and interests.
Lewin’s three-step model
provides the classic framework for managing planned change:

items.text: Unfreezing
— the status quo must be disturbed before old behaviour can be discarded; this often means making the need for change vivid and legitimate to those affected.
Movement
— the actual change to a new state takes place, as employees are guided through the new processes, structures, or behaviours.
Refreezing

— the new state must be reinforced (through supportive structures, culture, and reward systems) so the organization does not simply drift back to the old status quo once the initial pressure for change eases.

segments.text: Innovation is the process of taking a creative idea and turning it into a useful product, service, or method of operation. It is useful to distinguish invention (creating a new idea) from innovation (successfully applying that idea to create value), and to note that an organization’s ability to exploit creativity — turning ideas into actual products or process improvements — is what ultimately determines competitive advantage, not creativity in isolation.
Key takeaways

items.text: Resistance to change typically stems from uncertainty, fear of loss, or perceived misalignment with existing goals — effective change management addresses these root causes rather than simply overriding resistance.
Lewin’s three-step model — unfreeze, move, refreeze — highlights that change is not complete once the new behaviour appears; it must be actively reinforced or the organization risks reverting.
Innovation is the successful application of a creative idea to create value; organizations succeed not merely by generating ideas but by systematically exploiting them.

segments.text: Leadership is the ability to influence a group toward the achievement of a vision or set of goals — a capacity distinct from formal managerial authority, since one can be a manager without being an effective leader, and vice versa. Major theoretical traditions covered by the syllabus include:

items.text: Trait theories

, which sought to identify a fixed set of personal qualities (drive, self-confidence, honesty) that distinguish leaders from non-leaders — now understood to be, at best, a partial explanation, since traits alone do not guarantee effective leadership without the right situational fit.
Behavioural theories

, which shifted attention from who leaders are to what leaders do — most notably distinguishing task-oriented behaviour (structuring work and defining roles) from people-oriented (consideration) behaviour, and studying how these combine.
Contingency theories

(such as Fiedler’s model), which argue that a leadership style’s effectiveness depends on the situation — matching a task-oriented or relationship-oriented leader to situations that are more or less favourable for that style, rather than assuming one style is universally best.
Contemporary approaches
, including
transactional leadership
(leading primarily through the exchange of rewards for performance and correction of deviations) and
transformational leadership

(inspiring followers to transcend their own self-interest for the good of the organization, through a compelling vision and personal example) — the latter is generally associated with stronger, more sustained follower commitment.

segments.text: Motivation refers to the processes that account for an individual’s intensity, direction, and persistence of effort toward attaining a goal. The syllabus’s core theories are best remembered in two families:

items.text: Content theories
ask what motivates people.
Maslow’s hierarchy of needs
proposes five need levels (physiological, safety, social, esteem, self-actualization), arguing that lower needs must be substantially satisfied before higher ones become motivating.
Herzberg’s two-factor theory
distinguishes
hygiene factors
(salary, working conditions, company policy — their absence causes dissatisfaction, but their presence does not itself motivate) from
motivators

(achievement, recognition, responsibility — whose presence genuinely drives higher performance and satisfaction). The practical implication of Herzberg’s theory is important: simply improving hygiene factors (a bigger office, better pay alone) removes dissatisfaction but does not, by itself, increase motivation — true motivation requires attention to the job’s intrinsic content.
Process theories
ask how motivation happens.
Vroom’s expectancy theory

argues that an individual’s motivation to act in a certain way depends on the strength of the expectation that the act will be followed by a given outcome, and on the attractiveness of that outcome to the individual — captured in the relationship between effort → performance, performance → reward, and the value of the reward. If an employee doubts that effort will actually lead to good performance (poor training, inadequate resources), or that good performance will actually be rewarded (an unfair or arbitrary appraisal system), motivation collapses regardless of how attractive the reward itself might be.

segments.text: Key takeaways

items.text: Leadership theory has evolved from asking “what traits do leaders have?” to “what do leaders do?” to “which style fits which situation?” to today’s emphasis on transformational leadership, which builds commitment through vision rather than transaction alone.

Content theories (Maslow, Herzberg) explain what people need; process theories (Vroom) explain how the link between effort, performance, and reward determines whether that need actually translates into motivated behaviour.
Herzberg’s key practical insight — that hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction but do not themselves motivate — is one of the most exam-relevant single points in this entire unit.
